daisyworld.title: Daisyworld
daisyworld.subtitle: A planet that regulates its own temperature with no controller and no foresight
daisyworld.aria: A plot of planetary temperature against solar brightness: a living world's temperature stays nearly flat across a wide range while a bare lifeless world's temperature climbs straight through it
daisyworld.hintAlive: Slide the sun. Black daisies seize the cold early world and warm it; white daisies take the hot late world and cool it — and the planet's temperature barely moves while the bare-rock line climbs straight past. No daisy intends any of it.
daisyworld.hintDead: Past the daisies' limits the planet is bare rock again, and its temperature tracks the lifeless line exactly. The regulation only exists while life does.

habitableZone.title: The habitable zone
habitableZone.subtitle: Where liquid water can survive on a world's surface
habitableZone.hint: Drag the star's brightness and the distance to find the liquid-water band.

whittaker.title: Whittaker biome diagram
whittaker.subtitle: Temperature × rainfall decides which biome a climate grows
whittaker.hint: Drag the point — or use the sliders — to see which climate grows which biome. Pandora is warm and wet: rainforest runs wide.

circulationBands.title: Atmospheric circulation
circulationBands.subtitle: Spin rate sets the width of the Hadley cell
circulationBands.intro: The same law, two spin speeds. A slower spin weakens the Coriolis effect and widens the Hadley cell - so the equatorial rain belt swells and the deserts are pushed to high latitudes.
circulationBands.takeaway: The width of the cell sets the latitude of every forest and desert - and because Pandora spins slowly, its rainforest spreads across almost the whole world.

atmosphere.title: Atmosphere comparison
atmosphere.subtitle: The same oxygen push, a world of difference in CO₂ pressure
atmosphere.takeaway: The same oxygen push — but a world of difference in CO₂ pressure.

detectionScope.title: Detecting a world you cannot see
detectionScope.subtitle: Three windows onto the same orbiting planet
detectionScope.descRv: The planet tugs the star into a small wobble about their shared centre. As the star swings toward us then away, its light blue-shifts then red-shifts — a periodic wave that betrays a world we never see.
detectionScope.descTransit: When the planet crosses in front of the star, it blocks a sliver of light. The brightness dips and recovers on a clock — and the depth of the dip reveals the planet's size.
detectionScope.descImaging: Hide the star's glare behind a mask and you can photograph the faint dot of the planet beside it — the hardest method, but the one that truly sees a world.

eclipseClock.title: The daily eclipse clock
eclipseClock.subtitle: Polyphemus hangs fixed while the sun slides behind it
eclipseClock.hint: Drag time: Polyphemus hangs fixed in the sky while the sun slides behind it each late afternoon.

carbonateSilicate.title: The thermostat with no thermostat
carbonateSilicate.subtitle: How Earth stayed liquid under a sun 30% fainter
carbonateSilicate.co2Note: relative to today — high under a faint sun
carbonateSilicate.aria: Surface temperature against solar brightness: the regulated planet stays near liquid-water temperatures across the range while a bare rock scorches straight through.
carbonateSilicate.hintFaint: Under the faint young sun a bare rock would freeze solid — yet the thermostat lets CO₂ pile up, thickening the greenhouse until the planet stays liquid. This is why the early Earth never froze.
carbonateSilicate.hintBright: As the sun brightens, warmer rock in acid rain weathers faster, drawing CO₂ out of the air and thinning the greenhouse. The planet cools itself — the thermostat turning itself down with no one at the dial.

atmosphericDisequilibrium.title: Reading life off the air
atmosphericDisequilibrium.subtitle: A dead world settles; a living world is held impossible
atmosphericDisequilibrium.disequilibriumNote: reactive gases held coexisting — the biosignature
atmosphericDisequilibrium.deadPumpHint: Nothing to pump — the air has settled into chemical equilibrium
atmosphericDisequilibrium.aria: Atmospheric composition of the chosen world; the disequilibrium index reads {value}.
atmosphericDisequilibrium.hintDead: A dead world settles into chemical equilibrium — Mars and Venus are both more than 95% CO₂, inert and finished. There is nothing to pump and nothing out of balance, so a distant telescope reads: lifeless.
atmosphericDisequilibrium.hintAlive: Earth's air is impossible: reactive oxygen and methane coexisting, a mixture chemistry should erase. Only a ceaseless biological pump holds it open — and that disequilibrium, not any single gas, is the most robust signature of life we can read from afar.
